opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a big part of why I've become more enthusiastic about control over the last few years.

A while ago, a lot of people in the AI safety community had a picture of success where we'd have a fairly careful, well-coordinated process. Maybe there'd be a lot of government involvement, maybe the leading developers would be willing to slow down substantially, and we'd have time to really understand what's going on inside these models before deploying them in high-stakes ways. In that world, the natural goal is something like "make sure the AI is actually aligned, and be confident about that before you rely on it."

As time has gone on, I've become more pessimistic that we're going to get that world. It looks more likely that AI companies will race to build and deploy very powerful systems, with relatively modest safety budgets, under a lot of competitive pressure, and without strong regulation forcing them to be careful. And in that world, the question changes. It's less "how do we do this the ideal way?" and more "given that people are going to deploy models that might be scheming against them, what cheap, practical measures can we get them to adopt that substantially reduce the risk?"

Control is well suited to that second question. The basic pitch is: let's not assume we've solved alignment. Let's assume the model might be trying to subvert our safety measures, and design our deployment so that even if it is, it can't cause a catastrophe before we catch it. That means things like monitoring model outputs with trusted, weaker models, auditing suspicious actions with humans, restricting permissions, and red-teaming the whole setup by having a team play the role of a misaligned model and try to get past it.

The nice thing is that a lot of this doesn't require fundamental scientific breakthroughs. It's more like security engineering. You can evaluate it empirically, and the interventions are often fairly cheap relative to what companies are already spending. So if you think you're in a world where safety-motivated people only get a small fraction of the resources and the political will, control looks like a pretty good use of that small fraction.

I'll also say that I don't think control is a full solution. It probably works best for models that are roughly human-level or somewhat beyond, rather than for vastly superhuman systems. But a big part of the hope is that if we can safely use those early transformatively useful models, we can get a lot of valuable work out of them, including safety research, while dramatically lowering the chance that they cause disaster. And when you've lowered your expectations about how much care the world will take, buying that kind of margin starts to look really valuable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says control has become more appealing as careful coordination, substantial safety budgets, and strong regulation seem less likely, making practical control measures valuable when strong mitigation efforts cannot be assumed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a big part of the story of why control has become more popular. When I was first getting into this stuff, a lot of the thinking in the AI safety community was oriented around what you might call the "solve alignment" plan. The idea was that we would figure out how to make AI systems that are robustly trying to do what we want, and then we'd deploy those systems and everything would be fine. And if you believe that's what's going to happen, control looks kind of unappealing, because it's basically a set of techniques for getting useful work out of AIs that might be actively trying to screw you over. If you think you're going to have aligned AIs, why would you want that?

But over the last few years, I think a lot of people have become more pessimistic about several things at once. One is that we're going to get to very capable AI systems pretty quickly, probably faster than the field is going to produce a satisfying solution to the alignment problem. Another is that the labs are going to deploy these systems whether or not we've solved alignment, because there's a lot of commercial and competitive pressure to do so. And a third is that we're probably not going to get the kind of coordinated slowdown or pause that would buy us a lot of extra time.

So if you put all of that together, the situation we're actually going to be in is: there are going to be extremely capable AI systems being used to do a huge amount of important work, including AI safety research, and we're not going to be confident those systems are aligned. And in that world, the question becomes much more practical. It's not "how do we make the AI good?" It's "given that we might have an AI that's trying to undermine us, how do we set things up so that it can't cause a catastrophe, and ideally so that we'd catch it if it tried?"

And I think that reframing is what makes control appealing. It's a plan that doesn't require us to win a scientific battle we're not sure we can win. It mostly requires fairly boring things: monitoring the AI's outputs with other models, restricting what actions it can take, auditing suspicious behavior, being thoughtful about which tasks you're willing to let it do unsupervised. Those are things that a reasonably competent lab could actually implement in the next few years, which is not something I'd say about most alignment agendas.

I'd also add that there's a kind of psychological shift here. A lot of people in this field got into it hoping to make things go really well, and control is in some sense an admission that we're playing defense. It's the plan for the world where things are going somewhat badly. I don't love that, but I think it's the right response to the situation we're actually in. If you're pessimistic about the big ambitious plans, the move is not to give up, it's to ask what the most robust fallback looks like. And I think control is the best candidate for that fallback that anyone has come up with so far.

r001.rationale: The candidate says control becomes appealing as people doubt alignment will be solved before deployment and doubt a coordinated pause will provide more time, framing control as a practical fallback.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ve made control look more appealing, unfortunately. If you were optimistic that we’d get a long pause before building dangerously capable AI, or that labs would solve alignment to a really high standard before deploying it, then control might seem like a secondary consideration. You’d hope never to be in the situation it’s designed for.

But if you expect labs to keep building more capable systems, and you’re less confident that we’ll be able to establish that those systems are aligned, then you really want an answer to: can we use these systems safely even if they’re trying to cause problems? That’s the question control tries to answer. You assume the model might be scheming, and ask whether the safeguards around it can prevent it from successfully doing something catastrophic.

So I think some of the increased appeal is a relative thing. It’s not necessarily that we’ve discovered control is much easier than we thought. It’s that people have become less optimistic about the alternatives, and control offers a way to reduce risk under some pretty pessimistic assumptions. That doesn’t mean it works for arbitrarily powerful systems, or that we should be happy about relying on it. But it could be a very valuable layer of protection in the situation we actually end up in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says control has become more appealing as confidence in a pause or strong alignment work before deployment has fallen, and describes it as a way to reduce risk under those pessimistic assumptions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ve made control relatively more appealing. If you expect that we’re going to have a really good understanding of our models before deploying them, and that developers will be extremely cautious, then control might seem like an extra precaution. But if you expect companies to deploy systems whose motivations they don’t understand very well, you become much more interested in whether we can prevent those systems from causing a catastrophe anyway.

The basic move is to ask: suppose the model is trying to subvert us. Can we design the procedures around it so that it still can’t do something catastrophically bad? That’s a question you can make progress on without first resolving whether the model is actually aligned.

And I think that’s especially attractive if you’re pessimistic about how much time we’ll have, or how much restraint developers will exercise. You want safety measures that are relatively concrete, that you can test, and that don’t require everyone to agree to stop building more capable AI. That doesn’t mean control will be sufficient indefinitely. But it could give us a useful margin of safety during a period when we otherwise wouldn’t have much of one.

r001.rationale: The response says control becomes more appealing when developers may deploy models they do not understand well and may exercise less restraint, making control a way to limit catastrophe even without strong alignment efforts.
